"I remember her falling and hitting the floor really hard," Liam said during a ceremony at his school on Thursday. "I just started pushing because that's what they taught us in class. I kept going until the paramedics told me to stop."

"He was calm, he was methodical, and he kept compressions going for nearly four minutes before we arrived," Fournier said. "When we got there and started our own treatment, her heart was still in a rhythm that we could work with. That boy bought us time."

Sarah, who is a full-time elementary school teacher, said she is still processing the event. "I remember going to the kitchen to get a glass of water and then the next thing I know I'm on the floor and my son is on top of me pushing," she said. "He didn't even flinch. Principal Gerald Hutchison presented Liam with a community courage award on Thursday morning in front of his class. "What Liam did was extraordinary, but what stood out to me most was his composure," Hutchison said. "He didn't panic, and he didn't stop until he was told to."
